pages.text: One spring morning, Grandma took Lara to the potter’s workshop at the end of the village. “We need a new water jug,” said Grandma.
pages.speech: One spring morning, Grandma took Lara to the potter’s workshop at the end of the village. “We need a new water jug,” said Grandma.

pages.text: Inside, it smelled of wet earth. Jugs and bowls stood on every shelf. The potter sat at his wheel, and his hands were grey with clay.
pages.speech: Inside, it smelled of wet earth. Jugs and bowls stood on every shelf. The potter sat at his wheel, and his hands were grey with clay.

pages.text: On a low shelf by the window, little clay birds were drying in the sun. “Blow into their tails,” said the potter, “and they sing.”
pages.speech: On a low shelf by the window, little clay birds were drying in the sun. “Blow into their tails,” said the potter, “and they sing.”

pages.text: Grandma looked at jugs. The potter went back to his wheel. Lara picked up the smallest bird. It was cool and smooth. And then… it slipped.
pages.speech: Grandma looked at jugs. The potter went back to his wheel. Lara picked up the smallest bird. It was cool and smooth. And then… it slipped.

pages.text: Crack! The bird fell onto the workbench, and one wing broke off. Lara looked round. Nobody had seen. Her heart went thump, thump, thump.
pages.speech: Crack! The bird fell onto the workbench, and one wing broke off. Lara looked round. Nobody had seen. Her heart went thump, thump, thump.

pages.text: She could put the bird back on the shelf, with its broken side to the wall. Nobody would know. What do you think Lara will do?
pages.speech: She could put the bird back on the shelf, with its broken side to the wall. Nobody would know. What do you think Lara will do?

pages.text: Lara looked at the little wing in her hand. Then she picked up the bird, very gently. She carried it to the potter.
pages.speech: Lara looked at the little wing in her hand. Then she picked up the bird, very gently. She carried it to the potter.

pages.text: The wheel slowed down and stopped. “I dropped it,” said Lara, in a small voice. “I’m sorry.”
pages.speech: The wheel slowed down and stopped. “I dropped it,” said Lara, in a small voice. “I’m sorry.”

pages.text: The potter looked at her for a long moment. Then he smiled. “Thank you for telling me,” he said. “Come. Let’s mend it together.”

pages.text: He gave Lara a lump of soft, wet clay. Together they pressed it into the crack. They smoothed it with wet fingers, round and round.
pages.speech: He gave Lara a lump of soft, wet clay. Together they pressed it into the crack. They smoothed it with wet fingers, round and round.

pages.text: The wing was back on, a little bit crooked. The potter blew gently into the tail. And the bird sang a wobbly, happy song. Fee-oo-wee!

pages.text: Grandma came over with her new jug. “What a happy song!” she laughed. Lara blew into the tail too. Fee-oo-wee, fee-oo-wee.

pages.text: The potter put the bird back on the shelf. “Tomorrow it goes in the kiln, to make it strong,” he said. “Then it will wait here for you.”

activity.title: The Fix-It Table
activity.goal: Mend something broken, step by step.
materials: An old drawing or a magazine page

steps.caption: Tear the page into four big pieces.
Fit the pieces together, like a puzzle.

activity.safety: The grown-up tears off the strips of tape, and a tape dispenser with metal teeth stays in adult hands. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Lara breaks a clay bird and tells the potter. He thanks her, and they mend it together. Owning up is easier when it is met with thanks rather than anger. This activity practises the second half of the story: what is broken can often be mended, step by step. Tear an old drawing or a magazine page into four or five big pieces. The child fits them together like a puzzle, then tapes over the tears. Stay close and help with a question rather than the answer: “Where do you think this corner goes?” While you work, you can talk: “Have we ever broken something? What happened next?” And when the child tells you about a real mistake, thank them first, as the potter did, then fix it together. To make it easier, use three pieces. To make it harder, use eight pieces, or tear two pages and mix them up. Ten to fifteen minutes is plenty.
activity.inClass: Children work in pairs. The adults tear old pages beforehand and give each pair two torn pages. Each child mends their partner’s page, then they swap back and tell each other what the picture shows. The tape stays with the adults, who hand out the strips.
